packet.description_seed: Queen-cell wax helps shape honeybee queen development, challenging the idea that royal jelly alone makes a queen, a new study suggests.

what: A secret to making a queen bee may lie in the wax around it

clean_source_blocks.text: Queen-cell wax helps shape honeybee queen development, challenging the idea that royal jelly alone makes a queen, a new study suggests.

Queen bees emerge from special wax chambers Royal wax, as well as royal jelly, determines the fate of a honeybee larva by Soumya Sagar, special to C&EN The latest chemistry news, including important research advances, business and policy trends, chemical safety practices, career guidance, and more. A honeybee larva’s ascent to royalty is shaped by more than gobbling up royal jelly; it is also dictated by her cradle. Scientists have discovered that the queen cells are made of chemically engineered, “bespoke” wax that is critical for the survival and development of future queens (Nature 2026, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10534-3).

“For centuries, we believed ‘you are what you eat’ was the only rule for making a queen bee. Our study rewrites that rule to say ‘you are where you live, too,’” Kai Wang, a study co-author with the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, said in an email. The findings offer a rare look inside the hive, but questions remain. Honeybees pollinate and ensure the survival of crops such as blueberries, squash, watermelon and almonds. Further research is needed to learn more about the secret lives of queen cell-building bees and the exact combination of factors that produce the hive’s head honcho. “I would really like to know more about the specific chemical composition of this wax and which active ingredients are directly affecting the growth of the queens,” Bowsher said.

The wax of the peanut-shaped chamber where the queen develops has distinct physical and chemical properties that help steer its development, researchers report June 3 in Nature. By analyzing the chamber’s composition and the larvae it harbors, the team challenges the long-held notion that royal jelly alone — the queen-making food fed to select larvae — makes a queen.

[Lähde: Science News]
This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback?			
				Take our survey			.
			(See our AI policy 			
				here			.)

A queen bee may be shaped by more than its famous royal diet.

The wax of the peanut-shaped chamber where the queen develops has distinct physical and chemical properties that help steer its development, researchers report June 3 in Nature. By analyzing the chamber’s composition and the larvae it harbors, the team challenges the long-held notion that royal jelly alone — the queen-making food fed to select larvae — makes a queen.

“The discovery is very cool and thought-provoking,” says Thomas Seeley, a biologist at Cornell University who was not involved in the work. “To me, queen cells have long seemed important because odors from a developing queen may permeate the wax walls, marking them as very special spots that workers recognize and don’t accidentally damage.”

---

[Lähde: Orange County Register]
NEW YORK (AP) — Scientists have identified a group of worker honeybees that are specially adapted to build their queen’s waxy abode within the hive.

Worker bees perform a myriad of jobs to keep up the hive, including collecting food, nurturing young bees and caring for the queen, who lays all the eggs. New research reveals that the honeybees responsible for crafting the queen’s home effectively run a fever to help melt and blend special chemicals into the wax.

“No one had ever thought that there might be a specialized group of workers that were building these queen cells,” said bee researcher Julia Bowsher with North Dakota State University, who had no role in the study.

These newly identified bees were younger and also had patterns of expression in their genes that made them uniquely suited to the task. The resulting peanut-shaped home was also distinct in its makeup, as it was made of softer wax with a higher melting point than the kind used to build worker bees’ homes.

Queens are raised eating royal jelly secreted from the glands of worker bees and scientists have long believed diet was the main key to making a monarch. The new findings, published Wednesday in the journal Nature, suggest that the queen’s environment might also play a role.

To test that theory, researchers raised baby queens in cups capped with either queen or worker wax. Despite eating royal jelly, the queens raised in worker wax were smaller and didn’t survive as well.

“For centuries, we believed ‘you are what you eat’ was the only rule for making a queen bee. Our study rewrites that rule to say ‘you are where you live, too,’” Kai Wang, a study co-author with the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, said in an email.

The findings offer a rare look inside the hive, but questions remain.

Honeybees pollinate and ensure the survival of crops such as blueberries, squash, watermelon and almonds. Further research is needed to learn more about the secret lives of queen cell-building bees and the exact combination of factors that produce the hive’s head honcho.

“I would really like to know more about the specific chemical composition of this wax and which active ingredients are directly affecting the growth of the queens,” Bowsher said.

The Associated Press Health and Science Department receives support from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute’s Department of Science Education and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. The AP is solely responsible for all content.

[Lähde: C&EN]
Queen bees emerge from special wax chambers

Royal wax, as well as royal jelly, determines the fate of a honeybee larva

by 
			
				
				 
				 
				 Soumya Sagar, special to C&EN

The latest chemistry news, including important research advances, business and policy trends, chemical safety practices, career guidance, and more.

A honeybee larva’s ascent to royalty is shaped by more than gobbling up royal jelly; it is also dictated by her cradle. Scientists have discovered that the queen cells are made of chemically engineered, “bespoke” wax that is critical for the survival and development of future queens (Nature 2026, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10534-3).

For decades, the scientific consensus held that the larvae fed an exclusive diet of royal jelly grew into fertile, long-lived queens, while their sisters who got standard fare grew into sterile workers. Although nutrition is undeniably important, researchers suspected something else was also at play.

One place to look was the cells in which queen bees are reared. These are large, vertical wax cells, totally different from the classic hexagonal honeycomb of workers.

“Honeybees invest enormous effort in building highly specialized queen cells,” Boris Baer, an entomologist at the University of California, Riverside, says in an email. “From an evolutionary perspective, it seemed unlikely that such elaborate structures existed simply as containers for food.”

Baer and his collaborators investigated the physical and chemical properties of the queen cells and worker cells of western honeybees (Apis mellifera). They used scanning electron microscopy to examine the wax’s physical structure and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry to run a full chemical audit.

The researchers found that, compared with worker cell wax, queen cell wax is richer in unsaturated fatty acids, specifically oleic acid, linoleic acid, and α-linolenic acid, and poorer in n-alkanes, such as pentacosane, and wax esters. It also has a lower density, hardness, and mechanical strength (both tensile and compressive) than its worker counterparts and exhibits a significantly higher peak melting temperature.

Using a specialized tracking system with thermal imaging and high-definition lenses, the researchers monitored the bees’ construction activities and identified a dedicated crew of queen-cell builder bees who are significantly younger than their worker-cell-building counterparts. These builders physically overheat their bodies to nearly 40 °C

payload.title: Mehiläiskuningattaren kehityksessä voi ratkaista myös kennon vaha
payload.summary: Uusi Nature-lehdessä raportoitu tutkimus viittaa siihen, että mehiläiskuningattaren kehitystä ohjaa emomaitoruokinnan lisäksi myös erityisen kuningatarkennon vaha. Löydös tarkentaa pitkään vallinnutta käsitystä siitä, miten valituista toukista kasvaa pesän kuningattaria.
payload.content:
Mehiläiskuningattaren kehitys ei ehkä riipu vain kuuluisasta emomaidosta, vaan myös siitä vahasta, jonka sisällä toukka kasvaa. Nature-lehdessä 3. kesäkuuta raportoitu tutkimus kertoo, että kuningatarkennon vahalla on erottuvia fysikaalisia ja kemiallisia ominaisuuksia, jotka auttavat ohjaamaan tulevan kuningattaren kehitystä ja haastavat vanhan, pelkkään ravintoon nojaavan selityksen.

## Kuningatar syntyy erityisessä kennossa

Mehiläispesässä kuningattareksi valitut toukat kehittyvät tavallisuudesta poikkeavissa, muodoltaan maapähkinää muistuttavissa vahakammioissa. Perinteisesti kuningattaren syntyä on selitetty ennen kaikkea ravinnolla: valitut toukat saavat emomaitoa, jonka on ajateltu olevan ratkaiseva tekijä niiden erilaistumisessa.

Uusi tutkimus tarkentaa tätä kuvaa. Tutkijat analysoivat kuningatarkennon koostumusta ja siellä kehittyviä toukkia ja päätyivät siihen, että myös kennon materiaali vaikuttaa kehitykseen. Lähteiden mukaan kuningatarkennot rakentuvat kemiallisesti muokatusta, tarkoitukseen sopivasta vahasta, joka on tärkeää tulevien kuningatarten selviytymiselle ja kehitykselle.

## Vaha muuttaa käsitystä kehitysympäristöstä

Tutkimuksen tekijöihin kuuluva Kai Wang Kiinan maataloustieteiden akatemiasta kuvasi löydöstä muutoksena vanhaan ajatukseen: kuningattaren kohdalla merkitystä ei ole vain sillä, mitä toukka syö, vaan myös sillä, missä se elää. Näin tutkimus nostaa kehitysympäristön rinnakkain emomaidon kanssa.

Havainnot tarjoavat harvinaisen kurkistuksen pesän sisäiseen kehitykseen, mutta moni yksityiskohta on yhä avoinna. Erityisesti kuningatarkennon vahan tarkka kemiallinen koostumus ja sen vaikuttavat ainesosat vaativat lisätutkimusta. Vielä ei siis tiedetä täsmällisesti, mitkä vahan ominaisuudet vaikuttavat suoraan kuningattaren kasvuun ja miten ne toimivat yhdessä emomaidon kanssa.

## Pölyttäjien merkitys lisää kiinnostusta

Löydöksellä on laajempaakin merkitystä, koska tarhamehiläiset ovat tärkeitä pölyttäjiä monille viljelykasveille. Lähteissä mainitaan esimerkiksi mustikat, kurpitsat, vesimelonit ja mantelit, joiden selviytymistä mehiläisten pölytystyö tukee.

Mitä paremmin kuningattaren kehitystä ymmärretään, sitä tarkemmin voidaan hahmottaa myös pesän lisääntymisen ja jatkuvuuden ehtoja. Seuraavaksi tutkijoiden on selvitettävä, millainen kuningatarkennon vaha on kemiallisesti ja mitkä sen ainesosista todella ohjaavat tulevan kuningattaren kasvua.
summary_bullets: Tutkimus viittaa siihen, että kuningatarkennon vaha vaikuttaa mehiläiskuningattaren kehitykseen emomaidon lisäksi.
Kuningatarkennon vahalla on erottuvia fysikaalisia ja kemiallisia ominaisuuksia.
Vahan tarkka koostumus ja sen vaikutusmekanismit vaativat vielä lisätutkimusta.
payload.journalist_note: Artikkeli perustuu packetin neljään lähdelohkoon. Keskeiset tiedot ovat yhteneviä: tutkimus julkaistiin Nature-lehdessä 3. kesäkuuta ja koskee kuningatarkennon vahan vaikutusta mehiläiskuningattaren kehitykseen.

Queen-cell wax helps shape honeybee queen development, challenging the idea that royal jelly alone makes a queen, a new study suggests.

Queen bees emerge from special wax chambers Royal wax, as well as royal jelly, determines the fate of a honeybee larva by Soumya Sagar, special to C&EN The latest chemistry news, including important research advances, business and policy trends, chemical safety practices, career guidance, and more. A honeybee larva’s ascent to royalty is shaped by more than gobbling up royal jelly; it is also dictated by her cradle. Scientists have discovered that the queen cells are made of chemically engineered, “bespoke” wax that is critical for the survival and development of future queens (Nature 2026, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10534-3).

“For centuries, we believed ‘you are what you eat’ was the only rule for making a queen bee. Our study rewrites that rule to say ‘you are where you live, too,’” Kai Wang, a study co-author with the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, said in an email. The findings offer a rare look inside the hive, but questions remain. Honeybees pollinate and ensure the survival of crops such as blueberries, squash, watermelon and almonds. Further research is needed to learn more about the secret lives of queen cell-building bees and the exact combination of factors that produce the hive’s head honcho. “I would really like to know more about the specific chemical composition of this wax and which active ingredients are directly affecting the growth of the queens,” Bowsher said.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .) A queen bee may be shaped by more than its famous royal diet. The wax of the peanut-shaped chamber where the queen develops has distinct physical and chemical properties that help steer its development, researchers report June 3 in Nature. By analyzing the chamber’s composition and the larvae it harbors, the team challenges the long-held notion that royal jelly alone — the queen-making food fed to select larvae — makes a queen.
